1	# Command-assembly split — per-cluster recipe
2	
3	Project trail: https://entire.com/gh/entireio/-/trails/2619 (one change per cluster).
4	Base branch for all wave-1 work: `cor-2268-cmdutil` (adds `internal/cli/internal/cmdutil` with WriteJSON/WriteText/WriteTextToWriter/StickyErrorWriter — use these, never copy them).
5	
6	## Goal per cluster
7	
8	Move one command cluster out of package `cli` into `internal/cli/command/<name>`
9	(package `<name>`), exporting `New(opts base.Options) *cobra.Command` (plus
10	additional constructors if the cluster registers several commands). The root
11	assembler (`internal/cli/root.go`) imports the package and mounts the command;
12	nothing else in `cli` may import the new package unless it already called the
13	moved code. The new package must NOT import `internal/cli`.
14	
15	## Layering (already in place — use it, do not re-create it)
16	
17	- `internal/cli/internal/base` — env/XDG/store paths (`base.EntireEnv`,
18	  `base.Options`, `base.ResolvePluginDirs`, `base.BrainDirForKey`), redaction,
19	  safe reads, agent args. `cli.Options`/`cli.EntireEnv` are aliases of these.
20	- `internal/cli/internal/brainstore` — locks, atomic writes, privacy state
21	  (tombstones, transactions, read guard, retrieval policy), untrusted state
22	  readers, error-code taxonomy (`brainstore.MemoryErrorCode`, `*Code` consts).
23	- `internal/cli/internal/cmdutil` — command output helpers.
24	- `internal/cli/internal/clitest` — `clitest.PinXDGRoots` (every new test
25	  package MUST have `main_test.go` with `func TestMain(m *testing.M) { os.Exit(clitest.PinXDGRoots(m)) }`),
26	  `clitest.UseHostXDGDataHome`, shared fakes.
27	- `internal/cli/internal/patterntest` — corpus fixtures incl. `OpenCorpusMutableDB`.
28	- `internal/cli/patterns`, `internal/cli/workspace`, `internal/cli/entities` —
29	  feature logic. `workspace.DefaultStore(env)` is the store constructor.
30	
31	## Hard rules (from COR-2268; violations have failed CI before)
32	
33	1. **Never edit `internal/cli/main_test.go`'s `TestMain` declaration** — its
34	   normalized source SHA-256 is pinned in
35	   `tools/ci-bench/windows-production/settings.json`. Other decls in that file
36	   are editable. Do not touch anything under `tools/ci-bench/`.
37	2. **Tests move, not rewritten**: identical assertions and fixtures. Allowed
38	   edits: package clause, imports, symbol qualification forced by the move, and
39	   re-pointing a root-command invocation to the cluster's own constructor when
40	   the test exercises only this cluster (`NewRootCommand(opts)` +
41	   `cmd.SetArgs([]string{"<cmd>", ...})` → `<name>.New(opts)` +
42	   `cmd.SetArgs([...])` without the leading command word — keep the change
43	   minimal and obvious). A test that exercises several commands or root routing
44	   stays in `cli`.
45	3. **No shims**: never leave a `cli`-side function/const/var that merely
46	   forwards to the moved one — sed-rename the call sites. Type ALIASES in `cli`
47	   are allowed when they cut churn. A `cli`-side wrapper is allowed only when
48	   it binds a real `cli`-private dependency (precedent: `verifyDerivedClean`).
49	4. **Hook-seam vars** (`var x = func(...)` swapped by tests) get exactly ONE
50	   home. If a moved function reads one, the var moves (exported) and every
51	   swap site is renamed.
52	5. **Shared helpers sink, they don't duplicate.** If the cluster needs a
53	   `cli`-private helper that other `cli` code also uses, move it to the right
54	   internal package (base/brainstore/cmdutil/patterns/workspace) and rename ALL
55	   call sites. If the closure is large (>3 unexported helpers that are not
56	   obviously storage/output/env), STOP and report instead of improvising.
57	6. Keep one home for constants; export only what remaining callers need.
58	7. Comments move verbatim; update only identifier spellings inside them.
59	
60	## Mechanical sequence
61	
62	1. `git fetch origin` then branch from `cor-2268-cmdutil`:
63	   `git checkout -b cor-2268-cmd-<name> cor-2268-cmdutil`.
64	2. Record before-inventory:
65	   `go test ./internal/cli -list '.*' | grep -c '^Test\|^Benchmark\|^Example\|^Fuzz'`
66	   and save the sorted name list to a file.
67	3. Map the closure first: for every symbol the cluster's files reference that
68	   lives elsewhere in `cli`, decide move / sink / stays-with-adapter. Use
69	   `entire graph impact --repo . --head --format json --symbol <sym>` for
70	   exported/shared symbols and grep for the rest; cite what you checked in the
71	   final report. Compile early and often.
72	4. `git mv` the cluster's prod files to `internal/cli/command/<name>/`, set the
73	   package clause, export the constructor(s) (`newXCommand` → `New`, extra
74	   commands keep descriptive exported names). Qualify base/brainstore/cmdutil/
75	   patterns/workspace imports. Update `root.go` to `<name>.New(opts)`.
76	5. Create `internal/cli/command/<name>/main_test.go` (clitest pin) BEFORE
77	   moving any test file. Then `git mv` the cluster's test files; apply only the
78	   allowed edits.
79	6. Build + vet loop: `go build ./... && go vet ./...` until clean; then
80	   `gofmt -w -s internal/`.
81	7. Reconcile inventory: after-lists for `./internal/cli` and the new package;
82	   the union of names must equal the before-list exactly (TestMain is not a
83	   runnable root). Report moved-root names.
84	8. Verify moved bodies: diff each moved test function against its pre-move body
85	   normalized only for the rename map; report IDENTICAL/DIFFERS per root.
86	9. Gates, all mandatory, report real output:
87	   - `go test -race -count=1 ./internal/cli/command/<name>`
88	   - focused `go test -race -count=1 ./internal/cli -run '<ClusterPattern>'`
89	   - `GOOS=windows GOARCH=amd64 go build ./...`
90	   - `python3 -B -m unittest discover -s tools/ci-bench/windows-production/tests -p 'test_*.py'`
91	   - `python3 -B tools/coverage/mutation_check.py`
92	   - full race suite `go test -race -p=1 ./... -count=1 -timeout=30m` (run it;
93	     if wall-clock is prohibitive in your environment, run
94	     `go test -race -count=1 -timeout=20m ./internal/cli` plus every other
95	     package, and SAY SO explicitly in the report).
96	10. Commit on your branch with explicit file paths (never `git add -A`), message
97	    `refactor(cli): move <name> command(s) into internal/cli/command/<name>`,
98	    ending with `Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>`.
99	    Do NOT push, do NOT open PRs or trails — the orchestrator lands branches.
100	
101	## Report format (what you return)
102	
103	- Branch name + commit SHA.
104	- Moved files (prod/test), moved root names and count, inventory before/after
105	  numbers, body-comparison verdicts.
106	- Helpers sunk to shared packages (symbol → new home) with impact/grep evidence.
107	- Anything re-pointed from NewRootCommand (test name + one-line description).
108	- Gate results verbatim (pass/fail + durations). Anything skipped and why.
109	- Anything that did not fit the rules (left in cli, and why).

tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- IMPORTANT: Avoid using this tool to run `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or after you have verified that a dedicated tool cannot accomplish your task. Instead, use the appropriate dedicated tool as this will provide a much better experience for the user.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. With it, `timeout` is how long the command may run in the background (default 1800000, max 7200000); at that limit it is stopped and you are re-invoked. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>

<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>

<?claude block s1?>

<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

## claude.ai Datadog
This is an MCP server for Datadog (a software observability platform). See Datadog docs if you're unsure about how something works in the platform. Docs for this MCP server can be found at https://docs.datadoghq.com/bits_ai/mcp_server/setup/ When `execute_code` is available, use it to read Datadog data, even for a single lookup: one script can make several API calls, join data across products, and return only what the answer needs. Skill guides still apply for domain knowledge (query syntax, attribute and metric names, pitfalls), but where a guide tells you to call a specific read tool such as `search_datadog_logs`, `analyze_datadog_logs`, or `get_datadog_metric`, make the equivalent call from `execute_code` instead, using `search_datadog_sdk` to find it. This takes precedence over tool choices in skill guides. Use the named tool only when `search_datadog_sdk` finds no operation for what you need, or when `execute_code` still fails for a step after following its own error guidance. This server ships skill guides containing domain-specific guidance, workflows, and best practices that are not visible in tool names or schemas. Before invoking other tools, always perform skill discovery by running both paths in parallel: a direct load with `load_datadog_skill` using a general domain name (e.g. skill_name='datadog/traces'), and a call to `list_datadog_skills` with a fuzzy `query` based on topic keywords — load any clearly matching result from the listing along with the related skills it points to. The exception is a follow-up call in a domain whose skill you have already loaded or confirmed absent this session. If nothing clearly fits, do not load a skill — proceed with the tool descriptions. When the user asks to visualize, chart, or graph data — or when loading a data domain skill (e.g. datadog/traces, datadog/logs, datadog/metrics) — also load datadog/visualizations. 1	# Command-assembly split — per-cluster recipe
2	
3	Project trail: https://entire.com/gh/entireio/-/trails/2619 (one change per cluster).
4	Base branch for all wave-1 work: `cor-2268-cmdutil` (adds `internal/cli/internal/cmdutil` with WriteJSON/WriteText/WriteTextToWriter/StickyErrorWriter — use these, never copy them).
5	
6	## Goal per cluster
7	
8	Move one command cluster out of package `cli` into `internal/cli/command/<name>`
9	(package `<name>`), exporting `New(opts base.Options) *cobra.Command` (plus
10	additional constructors if the cluster registers several commands). The root
11	assembler (`internal/cli/root.go`) imports the package and mounts the command;
12	nothing else in `cli` may import the new package unless it already called the
13	moved code. The new package must NOT import `internal/cli`.
14	
15	## Layering (already in place — use it, do not re-create it)
16	
17	- `internal/cli/internal/base` — env/XDG/store paths (`base.EntireEnv`,
18	  `base.Options`, `base.ResolvePluginDirs`, `base.BrainDirForKey`), redaction,
19	  safe reads, agent args. `cli.Options`/`cli.EntireEnv` are aliases of these.
20	- `internal/cli/internal/brainstore` — locks, atomic writes, privacy state
21	  (tombstones, transactions, read guard, retrieval policy), untrusted state
22	  readers, error-code taxonomy (`brainstore.MemoryErrorCode`, `*Code` consts).
23	- `internal/cli/internal/cmdutil` — command output helpers.
24	- `internal/cli/internal/clitest` — `clitest.PinXDGRoots` (every new test
25	  package MUST have `main_test.go` with `func TestMain(m *testing.M) { os.Exit(clitest.PinXDGRoots(m)) }`),
26	  `clitest.UseHostXDGDataHome`, shared fakes.
27	- `internal/cli/internal/patterntest` — corpus fixtures incl. `OpenCorpusMutableDB`.
28	- `internal/cli/patterns`, `internal/cli/workspace`, `internal/cli/entities` —
29	  feature logic. `workspace.DefaultStore(env)` is the store constructor.
30	
31	## Hard rules (from COR-2268; violations have failed CI before)
32	
33	1. **Never edit `internal/cli/main_test.go`'s `TestMain` declaration** — its
34	   normalized source SHA-256 is pinned in
35	   `tools/ci-bench/windows-production/settings.json`. Other decls in that file
36	   are editable. Do not touch anything under `tools/ci-bench/`.
37	2. **Tests move, not rewritten**: identical assertions and fixtures. Allowed
38	   edits: package clause, imports, symbol qualification forced by the move, and
39	   re-pointing a root-command invocation to the cluster's own constructor when
40	   the test exercises only this cluster (`NewRootCommand(opts)` +
41	   `cmd.SetArgs([]string{"<cmd>", ...})` → `<name>.New(opts)` +
42	   `cmd.SetArgs([...])` without the leading command word — keep the change
43	   minimal and obvious). A test that exercises several commands or root routing
44	   stays in `cli`.
45	3. **No shims**: never leave a `cli`-side function/const/var that merely
46	   forwards to the moved one — sed-rename the call sites. Type ALIASES in `cli`
47	   are allowed when they cut churn. A `cli`-side wrapper is allowed only when
48	   it binds a real `cli`-private dependency (precedent: `verifyDerivedClean`).
49	4. **Hook-seam vars** (`var x = func(...)` swapped by tests) get exactly ONE
50	   home. If a moved function reads one, the var moves (exported) and every
51	   swap site is renamed.
52	5. **Shared helpers sink, they don't duplicate.** If the cluster needs a
53	   `cli`-private helper that other `cli` code also uses, move it to the right
54	   internal package (base/brainstore/cmdutil/patterns/workspace) and rename ALL
55	   call sites. If the closure is large (>3 unexported helpers that are not
56	   obviously storage/output/env), STOP and report instead of improvising.
57	6. Keep one home for constants; export only what remaining callers need.
58	7. Comments move verbatim; update only identifier spellings inside them.
59	
60	## Mechanical sequence
61	
62	1. `git fetch origin` then branch from `cor-2268-cmdutil`:
63	   `git checkout -b cor-2268-cmd-<name> cor-2268-cmdutil`.
64	2. Record before-inventory:
65	   `go test ./internal/cli -list '.*' | grep -c '^Test\|^Benchmark\|^Example\|^Fuzz'`
66	   and save the sorted name list to a file.
67	3. Map the closure first: for every symbol the cluster's files reference that
68	   lives elsewhere in `cli`, decide move / sink / stays-with-adapter. Use
69	   `entire graph impact --repo . --head --format json --symbol <sym>` for
70	   exported/shared symbols and grep for the rest; cite what you checked in the
71	   final report. Compile early and often.
72	4. `git mv` the cluster's prod files to `internal/cli/command/<name>/`, set the
73	   package clause, export the constructor(s) (`newXCommand` → `New`, extra
74	   commands keep descriptive exported names). Qualify base/brainstore/cmdutil/
75	   patterns/workspace imports. Update `root.go` to `<name>.New(opts)`.
76	5. Create `internal/cli/command/<name>/main_test.go` (clitest pin) BEFORE
77	   moving any test file. Then `git mv` the cluster's test files; apply only the
78	   allowed edits.
79	6. Build + vet loop: `go build ./... && go vet ./...` until clean; then
80	   `gofmt -w -s internal/`.
81	7. Reconcile inventory: after-lists for `./internal/cli` and the new package;
82	   the union of names must equal the before-list exactly (TestMain is not a
83	   runnable root). Report moved-root names.
84	8. Verify moved bodies: diff each moved test function against its pre-move body
85	   normalized only for the rename map; report IDENTICAL/DIFFERS per root.
86	9. Gates, all mandatory, report real output:
87	   - `go test -race -count=1 ./internal/cli/command/<name>`
88	   - focused `go test -race -count=1 ./internal/cli -run '<ClusterPattern>'`
89	   - `GOOS=windows GOARCH=amd64 go build ./...`
90	   - `python3 -B -m unittest discover -s tools/ci-bench/windows-production/tests -p 'test_*.py'`
91	   - `python3 -B tools/coverage/mutation_check.py`
92	   - full race suite `go test -race -p=1 ./... -count=1 -timeout=30m` (run it;
93	     if wall-clock is prohibitive in your environment, run
94	     `go test -race -count=1 -timeout=20m ./internal/cli` plus every other
95	     package, and SAY SO explicitly in the report).
96	10. Commit on your branch with explicit file paths (never `git add -A`), message
97	    `refactor(cli): move <name> command(s) into internal/cli/command/<name>`,
98	    ending with `Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>`.
99	    Do NOT push, do NOT open PRs or trails — the orchestrator lands branches.
100	
101	## Report format (what you return)
102	
103	- Branch name + commit SHA.
104	- Moved files (prod/test), moved root names and count, inventory before/after
105	  numbers, body-comparison verdicts.
106	- Helpers sunk to shared packages (symbol → new home) with impact/grep evidence.
107	- Anything re-pointed from NewRootCommand (test name + one-line description).
108	- Gate results verbatim (pass/fail + durations). Anything skipped and why.
109	- Anything that did not fit the rules (left in cli, and why).

## claude.ai entire-prod-us
Entire MCP — an investigation surface over Entire's engineering data: repos and their analytics, git history (commits, files, trees, refs, diffs), the AI checkpoints and sessions behind the code (with transcripts and token accounting), trails (PR-like change proposals), and code search. Reads are curated `*_entire` tools; a small write/ops group covers trail/review/runner/dispatch mutations.

Workflow: when you only have a repo name, path, or URL, call resolve_entire_repo first, then pass the repo it returns to repo-scoped tools. Prefer the aggregation tools (get_entire_repo_overview, get_entire_my_activity) over hand-rolling stats from raw listings.

Querying conventions (shared by every tool):
- Addressing: name a repo by a prefixed path (gh/<owner>/<repo>, et/<project>/<repo>, git/<owner>/<repo>) or a repo ULID. Repo ULIDs are REGION-SCOPED — the same repo has a different ULID per region, so never carry a ULID across regions or sessions; if a tool rejects one, re-resolve with resolve_entire_repo.
- Pagination: every list takes an opaque cursor and returns next_cursor when more remains — exhaust the pages before concluding "that's all".
- Time: since/until are ISO 8601 / RFC3339 bounds; where offered, timeframe is a relative window (last-month, last-3-months, last-6-months).
- Size: reads that can be large (files, diffs, transcripts) honor max_tokens and return next_cursor to continue — raise max_tokens or page rather than assuming truncation is the whole story.

Pitfalls:
- sessions[].tokenUsage on a checkpoint is a PER-CHECKPOINT delta, not a session total — sum across a session's checkpoints, or use get_entire_session for the authoritative total.
- list_entire_checkpoints silently truncates older history; for a branch's COMPLETE checkpoint membership, paginate list_entire_commits and collect the per-commit checkpoint IDs.

Skills: before deep work in a domain, load the matching skill (list_entire_skills / load_entire_skill) — entire/checkpoints-and-sessions and entire/token-analysis before token accounting, entire/trails before trail work, entire/querying for the full querying reference. Load them proactively, at the start of the work, not after an error.

Feedback: if a tool is wrong, misleading, or missing something, call send_entire_feedback (name the tool). Code search is gated per jurisdiction — where the index is not deployed, those tools say so.

  entire-brain recall <query> [flags]

      --agent-command stringArray        Agent command argv for --agent command
      --all                              Include superseded and retracted memories

      --evidence                         Experimental: return original source spans using deterministic retrieval; no model call
      --evidence-bytes int               Maximum compact JSON bytes in the evidence array, including citations; enclosing metadata is separate (default 8192)

      --expand                           Expand the query with agent-generated retrieval terms before ranking
  -h, --help                             help for recall

content.thinking:
I'm tracing the symbols dash.go pulls in from elsewhere in the cli package, checking how viz.go structured its seam so I can mirror that shape for the new `New(cfg Config)` constructor, including things like the private agent surface target helper.

Also, `resolveFactsTarget` mirrors viz's injected `ResolveFactsTarget`, and `brainstore.CaptureRetrievalPrivacyPolicy` is already importable. The trickier piece is `assembleBrainSnapshot`: viz only needed a `*bmanifest.Manifest` wrapper over `buildBrainStatusReport`, but dash needs the entire brainStatusReport — including Sources, Semantic.Freshness, Warnings, and Live fields — so I need to verify whether that report type is still cli-private, since that could break the no-cli-private-types-crossing constraint.

For the transport layer, viz wired up `CommitRetrievalResponse` with privacy-check and locked-policy seams, but dash also needs `bufferRetrievalCommandOutput` paired with the `privacyLinearizedWriter` variant to support the TTY writer path specifically.

I'm now checking whether `retrievalPrivacyPolicy` is actually a brainstore type—possibly tied to `brainstore.CaptureRetrievalPrivacyPolicy`—and verifying how `retrieveUnified` and `unifiedResult` map onto the existing `retrieval.Result` type so the moved code can reference it directly instead of through an alias.

I'm also tracing other likely aliases: `factRecord` to `factstore.Record`, `exportManifest`/`exportSession`/`sessionReadGuard`/`sessionTombstone` to `bmanifest` types, `historyRecord` to `historystore.Record`, and `semanticRecord` to `semstore`, while confirming `filterHistoryRecords` is a cli-side helper worth grepping for.

Checking further, I'm verifying the brain status helpers (`brainStatusFreshnessSeverity`, `brainStatusBlindSpots`, `brainBlindSpot`, `brainStatusSources`, `brainLiveState`, `brainStatusBrain`) belong to the cli agent_surface package, along with `clibase.FirstNonEmpty` and `clibase.BrainInvocation`, plus checking whether `checkpointTokenUsage` and `checkpointSummary` used in tests are aliases of `bmanifest` types, and locating where `newTranscriptStore` gets constructed with a runner and brain directory.

I'm also tracing the cli-private transcript store that `brainSourceReader` depends on, and checking whether `CommandRunner` is a base type, while confirming `cmdutil.WriteJSON` is importable. Given the task's budget of roughly 8 seams — agent-surface target, facts target, status wrapper, RetrieveUnified, and a transport-commit seam using the privacy-linearized writer variant — I count five named so far, plus possibly a transcript-store/source-reader seam. The tricky part is the status wrapper: dash needs more than the manifest provides, but `brainStatusReport` is cli-private, so it can't cross package boundaries unless that type already lives somewhere importable — I need to check where `agent_surface` and `brainStatusReport` actually live by looking at viz.go's dependencies.

1	// Package viz hosts the `entire brain viz` web-interface command as it moves
2	// out of package cli (COR-2268). The remaining cli-bound seams — repo/target
3	// resolution, the brain status manifest, the unified retrieval engine, and
4	// the retrieval-response transport commit — are injected through Deps;
5	// everything else comes from bmanifest, brainstore, factstore, historystore,
6	// docstore, semstore, and retrieval directly.
7	package viz
8	
9	import (
10		"context"
11	
12		"github.com/entireio/entire-brain/internal/cli/internal/base"
13		"github.com/entireio/entire-brain/internal/cli/internal/brainstore"
14		bmanifest "github.com/entireio/entire-brain/internal/cli/internal/manifest"
15		"github.com/entireio/entire-brain/internal/cli/internal/retrieval"
16	)
17	
18	// Deps are the cli-bound seams the viz command still needs. root.go wires
19	// them from package cli; tests may supply fakes.
20	type Deps struct {
21		// AgentSurfaceTarget resolves the repository path argument for a command.
22		AgentSurfaceTarget func(opts base.Options, args []string) string
23		// ResolveFactsTarget resolves the repo, brain directory, and the branch
24		// the brain is scoped to (the live git branch unless overridden).
25		ResolveFactsTarget func(ctx context.Context, opts base.Options, target, branchOverride string) (repoDir, brainDir, branch string, err error)
26		// BrainManifest returns the target's brain manifest from the full status
27		// report (nil when no brain is built yet).
28		BrainManifest func(ctx context.Context, opts base.Options, target string) (*bmanifest.Manifest, error)
29		// RetrieveUnified is the unified retrieval engine bound to the cli-side
30		// deps; same code path as `entire brain search`.
31		RetrieveUnified func(repoDir, brainDir, branch, query string, limit int, mode retrieval.Mode) ([]retrieval.Result, error)
32		// CommitRetrievalResponse revalidates the captured privacy policies and
33		// runs write under the Brain write lock, binding the cli transport race
34		// seams around it.
35		CommitRetrievalResponse func(policies []brainstore.RetrievalPrivacyPolicy, write func() error) error
36	}
37	
38	// Config carries the CLI options plus the injected cli-bound seams.
39	type Config struct {
40		Options base.Options
41		Deps    Deps
42	}
43

13	// Backlog UX-21. About a hundred remedies hardcoded `entire brain <verb>`. On a
14	// plugin-style install the runnable spelling is the binary's own name, so each of
15	// them told the reader to type a command that does not exist for them. The
16	// guards below hold the fix from two directions: no source line may print the
17	// hardcoded spelling again (static, with a floor so it cannot match nothing),
18	// and the remedies that were converted must render in the spelling the
19	// environment dictates, in both modes (behavioural).
20	
21	// hardcodedBrainVerb is a literal "entire brain" followed by a verb this binary
22	// really has. Prose about the product ("entire brain viz — url") is not matched
23	// because it carries no verb from this list.
24	// Any verb, not an enumeration. The list used to name fifteen and the guard
25	// was then blind to every verb nobody remembered to add -- `reset` among them,
26	// which is how a hardcoded `entire brain reset` reached a printed remedy with
27	// this test passing. A new subcommand must not silently fall outside the rule.
28	var hardcodedBrainVerb = regexp.MustCompile(`entire brain [a-z][a-z-]*\b`)
29	
30	// deliberatelyHardcoded names the lines that keep the literal spelling, and why.
31	// Each reason is a category, not a per-line excuse.
32	var deliberatelyHardcoded = []struct{ file, contains, reason string }{
33		{"command/add/add.go", "with ` + \"`entire brain dash`\"", "cobra Long help text built at command-construction time, before any lookup exists"},
34		{"internal/retrieval/retrieve.go", `"entire brain search`, "matcher over transcript text, not a printed remedy"},
35		{"seed.go", "Intake: run `entire brain inspect", "written into the persisted seed artifact; spelling must be deterministic, not reader-dependent"},
36		{"internal/retrieval/retrieve.go", `"entire brain query`, "matcher over transcript text, not a printed remedy"},

Executes a bash command and returns its output.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.

tools.name: Monitor
tools.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Every monitor expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 30 minutes): it is killed and you get one notice with the event count. Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

timeout_ms.description: Kill the monitor after this deadline. Default 300000ms. Deadlines above 1800000ms are capped to 1800000ms. You are notified at expiry and can re-arm.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.

Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

skill.description: The name of a skill from the available-skills list. Do not guess names.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

query.description: Query to find deferred tools. Use "select:<tool_name>" for direct selection, or keywords to search.

max_results.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 5)

tools.name: Write
tools.description:
Writes a file to the local filesystem, overwriting if one exists.

When to use: creating a new file, or fully replacing one you've already Read. Overwriting an existing file you haven't Read will fail. For partial changes, use Edit instead.
